paragraphs.source_en: We have no detailed climatic record for the Tassili but the conditions were probably similar to the neighbouring Acacus. The Tassili is higher by circa 500 m, so that precipitation may have fallen in the form of snow and the climate would have been seasonally very cold. However, people could still live at a lower altitude. The climatic record suggests that life was possible in the mountainous regions from at least the 16th millennium BP. From the 10th millennium BP, when precipitation in the mountains diminished and the lakes in lowlands formed, important changes were likely to have occurred thanks to the possibility of human and animal mobility throughout the whole Sahara. The 10th millennium BP therefore appears to be the most probable starting point for the representation of the Round Head animals, especially of the water-dependent ones.

paragraphs.source_en: The large fauna may have persisted in the Central Sahara until the 6th millennium BP when the climate was still wet. After this date it became increasingly dry and water-dependent animals no longer survived the changing climate. The only large wild animals able to survive were the antelope and mouflon, still present within the region.

paragraphs.source_en: One of the main supporters of the low chronology, Muzzolini (1995a, b), claims that the representations of the large wild African fauna correspond with the last significant humid phase, i. e. the Neolithic period at 7,000 BP. His hypothesis is based on the conviction that the Round Head art contains images of domesticated animals and it must have therefore been created by Pastoral groups. Although the climatic conditions at 7,000 BP were suitable for the large African fauna to live in the Central Sahara and therefore to have been depicted in the rock art, Muzzolini's conclusions negate the artistic activity preceding the Neolithic period, which is in sharp contradiction to the archaeological record.
